_format: Original items. {1}, {2}, {3} mark blanks. In each blank's option list the FIRST option is correct; options are shuffled when served.

items.text: Although the critic was known for her {1} reviews, she praised the debut novel lavishly, calling it the finest of the decade.
items.clue: "Although" sets her usual reviews against lavish praise.
items.explanation: "Although" signals a contrast with praising lavishly, so her usual reviews must be harsh. Vitriolic means full of bitter criticism. Effusive and laudatory agree with the praise instead of contrasting with it; verbose and anonymous create no contrast at all.

items.text: The senator's {1} answers, which committed her to nothing, frustrated reporters who wanted a clear position on the bill.
items.clue: The answers "committed her to nothing."
items.explanation: Answers that commit to nothing and frustrate people wanting a clear position are deliberately vague: equivocal. Candid is the opposite; succinct, erudite, and impetuous don't describe noncommittal answers.

items.text: Far from being {1}, the new manager spent her first month asking employees for feedback and adopting many of their suggestions.
items.clue: "Far from being" means the blank is the opposite of what she did.
items.explanation: "Far from being" means the blank is the opposite of her behavior. She asked for and adopted others' ideas, so she was far from domineering: imperious. Amenable and receptive describe what she actually was; diligent and punctual aren't opposites of seeking feedback.

items.text: Scientists were initially {1} about the reported discovery, since the lab had a history of results that later proved impossible to replicate.
items.clue: The lab's history of results that couldn't be replicated.
items.explanation: A lab whose results often fail to replicate gives scientists reason to doubt it, so they were incredulous (unwilling to believe). Sanguine, effusive, and zealous are all positive reactions; credulous, too ready to believe, is the opposite of what the evidence supports.

items.text: The novelist's later work is notably {1}: where her early books sprawled across hundreds of pages, her recent stories rarely exceed a dozen.
items.clue: The colon: the second half explains the blank.
items.explanation: The colon introduces the explanation: the later stories are short where the early books sprawled, so the later work is succinct. Prolix describes the early books, not the later ones; ornate, esoteric, and derivative say nothing about length.

items.text: Because the treaty's language was so {1}, both nations could claim that it supported their opposing interpretations.
items.clue: Two opposing interpretations, both supported by the same text.
items.explanation: Only language open to more than one reading lets two nations claim opposite interpretations: ambiguous. Explicit language would rule that out. Verbose or archaic language isn't necessarily open to two readings, and bellicose doesn't fit.

items.text: The mayor's attempt to {1} the striking workers backfired: the small concessions she offered struck them as insulting rather than conciliatory.
items.clue: "Backfired" plus concessions that were meant to be conciliatory.
items.explanation: Concessions meant to be conciliatory show that she was trying to calm the workers: placate. "Backfired" means the opposite happened, and they were insulted. Provoke and castigate were not her aim; exonerate and galvanize don't match offering concessions.

items.text: Known as a {1} judge, she never once issued a ruling without first reading every brief twice.
items.clue: "Reading every brief twice."
items.explanation: Reading every brief twice before ruling shows careful attention to detail: meticulous. Lackadaisical and perfunctory mean the opposite, capricious means unpredictable, and pragmatic says nothing about thoroughness.

items.text: Critics who had dismissed the theory as merely {1} were forced to reconsider when three independent laboratories reproduced its central prediction.
items.clue: "Dismissed as merely," then overturned by independent confirmation.
items.explanation: Critics dismissed the theory, and independent confirmation forced them to reconsider, so they had considered it unproven: speculative. Corroborated and empirical describe what it turned out to be, and venerable and pragmatic aren't dismissive.

items.text: The biography is anything but {1}; the author, who clearly admires her subject, nonetheless records his cruelties as carefully as his triumphs.
items.clue: "Admires her subject" but "nonetheless" records his cruelties.
items.explanation: An admiring author might be expected to idealize her subject, but she "nonetheless" records his cruelties, so the book is anything but idealizing: hagiographic. It is balanced and meticulous, which makes "anything but" wrong for those words; derivative and abstruse aren't supported.

items.text: Though the region's climate is generally {1}, sudden spring storms can turn its rivers into torrents within hours.
items.clue: "Though" contrasts the general climate with sudden violent storms.
items.explanation: "Though" sets the usual climate against sudden violent storms, so it is usually mild: benign. Volatile and tempestuous agree with the storms rather than contrasting with them; humid and frigid don't contrast with storminess.

items.text: The once-{1} town, where nobody locked their doors, grew wary of strangers after a string of burglaries.
items.clue: "Nobody locked their doors" before it "grew wary."
items.explanation: Unlocked doors and the shift to wariness show the town used to be trusting. Suspicious describes it now; parochial, prosperous, and cosmopolitan aren't supported by the unlocked doors.

items.text: The professor's lectures were notoriously {1}, yet her written work was so {2} that even first-year students found it easy to follow.
items.clue: "Yet" contrasts the lectures with writing that is "easy to follow."
items.explanation: "Easy to follow" makes blank (ii) accessible. "Yet" sets the lectures against that, so they were hard to understand: abstruse. Lucid would remove the contrast, and brief isn't the opposite of easy to follow.

items.text: Initially {1} about the merger, the board grew enthusiastic once projections showed it would {2} the company's chronic cash shortages.
items.clue: "Initially … grew enthusiastic" shows a change of attitude.
items.explanation: The board "grew" enthusiastic, so it started out less than enthusiastic: ambivalent (sanguine and zealous are already positive). The projections must show something good about the shortages, so the merger would alleviate them. Exacerbate is the opposite, and merely concealing them wouldn't justify enthusiasm.

items.text: Although the diplomat's manner was unfailingly {1}, her colleagues knew that beneath the courtesy lay an {2} determination that no amount of pressure could shake.
items.clue: "Beneath the courtesy" and "no amount of pressure could shake."
items.explanation: "Beneath the courtesy" tells you her manner was friendly: affable (truculent is the opposite; diffident means shy). A determination that no pressure could shake is unyielding: obdurate. Irresolute and ephemeral contradict "could not be shaken."

items.text: The study's conclusions, once considered {1}, now appear {2}: subsequent research has exposed serious flaws in its methods.
items.clue: "Once … now" plus exposed flaws.
items.explanation: Exposed flaws mean the conclusions now look plausible but wrong: specious. "Once … now" signals a reversal, so they were once thought beyond challenge: unassailable. Dubious would mean no reversal happened, and preliminary isn't the opposite of specious.

items.text: Rather than {1} the minor errors in the report, the editor chose to {2} them, reasoning that a public correction would draw more attention to the mistakes than the mistakes themselves had.
items.clue: Her reasoning: a public correction would draw more attention.
items.explanation: She avoided a public correction because it would draw attention, so the rejected option is publicizing the errors, and what she chose was to disregard them. Overlook in blank (i) would make the two halves say the same thing; excoriate and amplify would draw the attention she wanted to avoid.

items.text: Her {1} approach to the restoration, cleaning each tile by hand and documenting every crack, meant the project took years longer than the {2} schedule the city had published.
items.clue: Hand-cleaning each tile; the project ran years over.
items.explanation: Cleaning each tile by hand and documenting every crack is meticulous work (cavalier is the opposite; pragmatic misses the point). Running years over means the city's schedule was too optimistic: sanguine. Punctilious and exorbitant don't describe an unrealistically short schedule.

items.text: The candidate's speeches were {1} enough to rouse even {2} voters, many of whom had not bothered to vote in decades.
items.clue: Voters who "had not bothered to vote in decades."
items.explanation: Voters who hadn't bothered to vote in decades are apathetic. Speeches that "rouse" even them are galvanizing; soporific and equivocal speeches wouldn't rouse anyone. Zealous or partisan voters wouldn't need rousing.

items.text: What first looked like {1} in the data turned out to be a genuine pattern; the effect appeared again in every {2} experiment.
items.clue: "First looked like … turned out to be a genuine pattern."
items.explanation: It "turned out" to be a genuine pattern, so at first it looked like a one-off: an anomaly (a trend would already be a pattern). It was confirmed because it appeared again in every later experiment: subsequent. Flawed or hypothetical experiments couldn't confirm it.

items.text: The committee's report was a model of {1}: in a mere four pages it {2} a problem that earlier studies, for all their length, had only {3}.
items.clue: "A mere four pages" against earlier studies "for all their length."
items.explanation: Four pages, praised as a model, means concision. "For all their length … had only" contrasts the long studies' failure with the report's success: the report elucidated (made clear) what the earlier studies only obscured. Clarified or solved in blank (iii) would remove the contrast.

items.text: Known for her {1} temperament, the coach shocked her players when she {2} them after a narrow loss; those who had played for her longest insisted that such outbursts were {3} rather than typical.
items.clue: "Shocked," "outbursts," and "rather than typical."
items.explanation: "Such outbursts" makes blank (ii) upbraided (scolded). It "shocked" the players, so her usual temperament was calm: placid (volatile and truculent would make the outburst unsurprising). "Rather than typical" makes blank (iii) aberrations.

items.text: Investors were {1} by the startup's early growth, but a closer look at its finances revealed that the gains were largely {2}, produced by one-time sales rather than a {3} customer base.
items.clue: "But a closer look" and "one-time sales rather than …"
items.explanation: "But a closer look revealed" means investors had been impressed at first: dazzled. Gains from one-time sales don't last, so they were ephemeral (one-time sales aren't fraud). "Rather than" sets one-time sales against a lasting, durable customer base.

items.text: The author's {1} prose, dense with allusions only specialists would catch, has won her {2} following among scholars but has done little to {3} the general readers her publisher hoped to attract.
items.clue: "Allusions only specialists would catch" and the readers the publisher "hoped to attract."
items.explanation: Prose full of allusions only specialists catch is recondite (obscure); pellucid and pedestrian are the opposite. "Won her" a following among scholars implies a devoted one ("no following" contradicts "won"). "But … done little to" attract general readers makes blank (iii) entice.

items.text: Despite the scientist's {1} claims that the drug was a {2}, the trial data showed that it merely {3} symptoms without curing the disease.
items.clue: "Despite" plus "merely … without curing."
items.explanation: "Despite" contrasts the claims with a modest result, so the claims were exaggerated: grandiose, that the drug was a cure-all, a panacea. In fact it merely palliated (eased) symptoms without curing. Exacerbated would make it harmful, not just disappointing.
